rv.q: Honestly, a lot of this change is carried by the charm of Whitfield and his chemistry with his co-star Buckland.
But the story simply doesn’t need them, isn’t built to accommodate them, loses pace when the singing starts.
The costumes sparkle but a production that needs Valentino swagger ends up being closer to John Lewis.
Come for the frocks and the folks, rather than the music and moves.
As a musical it’s pretty and uninteresting, shot through with the kind of obviousness and mediocrity that Miranda Priestly would abhor.
this show doesn’t really have a soul of its own
Sparkly as it is, I fear Miranda would hang it back on the rail.
This lacks both of those qualities.
The Devil Wears Prada is truly diabolical.
Generic songs, a derivative script and a daunting act to follow add up to a film-to-stage adaptation that’s shiny but skimpy
The Devil Wears Prada is a spectacular musical that successfully translates the essence of the classic film to the stage.

London’s West End has a new and fripperous, flouncy, fun-fest, just in time for Christmas, and it would take the stoniest of Yuletide curmudgeons not to enjoy an evening in the company of this most colourful of kaleidoscopic concoctions.
...a blend of awe-inspiring spectacle, sharp wit, and occasionally uneven storytelling
There is a strong score from Elton John, music with a beat that fuels choreography by director Jerry Mitchell that can combine catwalk prancing with highly camp abandon.
For now, it’s a musical worth seeing—just don’t expect to be completely swept off your feet.
When the musical embraces camp, it does it well.
The real subject of the story is workplace bullying, which it promotes as a moral virtue.
Here, as elsewhere, you get the feeling of a production too often settling for the generic when only true gorgeousness will do.
The production is distinctly lacking in memorable tunes or truly witty lines.
Sadly, this new stage adaptation has settled for mediocrity.
And yes, it was worth making a musical of the film: worth another dose of the shiny , fabulous and curiously wise nonsense of it.
Like Miranda Priestly herself, the Devil Wears Prada knows what it is and what it wants, and you’re certainly not going to stand in its way.
There is much to love about The Devil Wears Prada but there is also more that could have been done to make this more substantial rather than solely stylish.
The Devil Wears Prada musical doesn't completely sing.
Were it not for the hard work of a stellar cast and crew and its enjoyable musical numbers, it might be lost in a sea of stiff competition.

cn.t: The musical adaptation receives mixed reviews, with critics praising the lavish costumes and staging but finding the show lacks soul and purpose beyond replicating the beloved film. Elton John's score divides opinion.
